articleTitle: Preliminary Mid-Band Troposcatter Measurement Results Using Different High-Gain Receiver Antennas
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This article provides initial results of measurements made to assess the influence that different antenna patterns have on the received signal level of a mid-band troposcatter radio link. Measurements were performed at 3.475 GHz over a 185 km troposcatter link in Colorado with two vertically polarized receiver antennas: standard gain horn and parabolic dish. Median values of basic transmission loss (BTL) are compared for the two antennas. Cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) of hourly median BTL are plotted against predictions from the Institute for Telecommunications Sciences, Irregular Terrain Model (ITM). BTL measurements with the standard gain horn (219.77 dB median and 8.73 dB standard deviation) show better comparison with ITM predictions (214 dB median., and approximately 7.8 dB standard deviation) than BTL measurements made with the parabolic dish (228.21 dB median and 8.67 dB standard deviation). Further measurements and modeling are needed to explain these differences.

articleTitle: An Improved-Accuracy Discrete Sampling Criterion for the Estimation of the Local Mean Voltage of a Mobile Radio Channel
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper presents new recommendations for the discrete sampling of a mobile radio with non-line-of-sight Rayleigh fading and a Jakes power spectrum. The results are derived from a new analytical result for the variance of the local-mean voltage using discrete, spatial sampling with uniform spacing. The variance presented here accounts for the correlation between the samples and significantly changes the number of samples that are required to estimate the local mean voltage with a 1 dB spreading factor.

articleTitle: Evaluating the MR Safety of Passive Implants in Surgical and After Heal Models at 1.5 T and 3 T MRI
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Patients with medical implants may have contraindications when undergoing an MRI scan due to the accumulation of heat in tissues surrounding the implants. The heating of local tissue is due to the RF-fields from the MRI RF coil. Traditionally, the implant was first studied in the ASTM phantom having a uniform tissue medium wherein the electric fields will be uniform. This method can provide us the behavior of implant only under uniform electric fields exposure. In general, the human body has heterogenous tissues can lead to non-uniform incident electric field.

articleTitle: Significant Wave Height Estimation Using UAV
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper focuses on sea surface roughness estimation using the vertical electromagnetic (EM) field measured by an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV). For the purpose of measuring the signal, an embedded software-defined radio (SDR) based EM payload was constructed. This includes a custom-built front end composed of a low noise amplifier-limiter circuit. This drone receiver system was deployed at the Coastal Land-Air-Sea Interactions (CLASI) campaigns in Monterey, CA in 2021 and Santa Rosa, FL in 2023. The transmitters were deployed on buoys that simultaneously measured the significant wave height (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$H_{s}$</tex>). From the measured drone profiles, a significant wave height estimate was created and compared to the ground truth <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$H_{s}$</tex> values from the buoys. Inversion results indicated that estimation is feasible with further exploration to be done.

articleTitle: Scattering by an Octant-Sphere Located Inside a Trihedral Reflector
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The scattering of a plane wave of arbitrary polarization that is obliquely incident on an octant of a sphere whose center is located on the intersection of three faces of a trihedral metal reflector is considered. The analysis is conducted in the phasor domain with a time-dependence factor exp(+jwt) omitted throughout.

articleTitle: Broadband GaN MMICs for Analog Interference Suppression
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Receivers are subject to unwanted signals from both internal and external sources, which can overload the electronics, i.e. the analog to digital converter (ADC). Traditionally, this problem is addressed by using filters, but for broadband systems, these signals are no longer always out-of-band so a different, tuneable solution is needed. One solution is an interferometer topology. This topology, whose block diagram shown in Fig. 1(a), splits the incoming signal into two paths, adjusts the phase and magnitude of the paths, and recombines the paths so they are of the same magnitude and 180° out of phase so there is destructive interference and a spectral notch at a specific frequency. The phase delay is adjusted through the use of an artificial transmission line that used transistors as varactors. The proof of concept was shown in a GaAs MMIC across 6–12 GHz (P. Danielson, et al., “GaAs MMIC Inteferometer for Broadband Interference Suppression,” 2022 17th European Microwave Integrated Circuits Conf., Milan, Italy). To address the need for better linearity and higher power handling need when higher power unwanted signals are present, a hybrid circuit GaN version across 2–4 GHz with no gain is shown in (M. Robinson, et al., “Linear Broadband Interference Suppression Circuit Based on GaN Monolithic Microwave Integrated Circuits,” IET Circuits, Devices, and Systems, vol. 17, no. 4, Jul. 2023). This work presents two fully monolithically integrated solutions in WIN Semiconductors' NP15 GaN process that improve on previously published versions by using noise matched amplifiers to achieve low noise figure and GaN for high power handling and linearity.

articleTitle: The Sensitivity of RF Propagation to Stable Atmospheric Surface Layer Properties
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Electromagnetic wave propagation is affected by the atmospheric refractivity profile, the lowest 100 m of which is known as the atmospheric surface layer. This layer is dominated by the impacts of the surface itself. This study focuses on the surface layer over the ocean. Due to the evaporation from the ocean surface, a strong gradient in water vapor can form in this layer causing greatly increased detection ranges for sensors and targets within this gradient layer. When the lower atmosphere is driven by a warm ocean with a layer of cooler and drier air mass above, the result is an unstable surface layer. However, when a warm dry air mass moves over cooler water, the stable surface layer forms whose characteristics are much less predictable compared to the unstable surface layer. In this research, there is particular interest in the properties of the evaporation ducts in both the stable and unstable surface layers and how they impact radio frequency (RF) propagation.

articleTitle: Signal Compression with Waves
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Signal compression is one of the most important operations in systems that are used to store or transmit information, since it allows efficient use of the available bandwidth or storage capacity. A typical compression system, such as those that are used in the JPEG standard, involves a linear matrix operation, like the discrete wavelet transform, followed by a series of nonlinear operations, such as quantization of the signal and application of a code. As in many other instances of signal processing systems, the matrix operation is the most computationally demanding one since its complexity scales nonlinearly with the size of the input data. Therefore, compression systems would benefit significantly if the involved matrix operation could be implemented in the analog domain and in a parallel manner without the use of active components.

articleTitle: Development of the Ambipolar Electric Field in a Compressed Current Sheet and the Impact on Magnetic Reconnection
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Current sheets are important to space and laboratory plasmas, and particularly to the Earth's magnetotail, where during active periods, the solar wind compresses the magnetosphere creating thin current sheets. As a current sheet with a reversed magnetic field configuration is compressed, magnetic reconnection can occur, which causes field lines to snap, shooting a mesoscale plasma depolarization front towards Earth. This process can affect the plasma state of the magnetotail, driving space weather and injecting energetic particles into the radiation belts, which impacts Earth orbiting satellites.

articleTitle: Scattering from a Forest with an Underlying Rough Surface
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The NASA JPL AirSAR with P, L and C band radars flew over a hemlock forest in the summer of 1989. A ground crew of NASA personnel and George Washington (GW) participants made extensive canopy and ground truth measurements in the week before the flights. Tree trunks, branches and needles were measured as well as soil roughness profiles over a site that was 200m by 200m. The SAR backscattering coefficients were computed using Distorted Born Approximation (DBA). The surprising results showed that only the C band cross sections agreed with the SAR data. The P and L band theoretical results were 8 to 9 dBs too low. The results of the ground truth data collection and theory are given in Chauhan, et.al., IEEE Trans on Geosci. Remote Sens., Vol 29, pp 627-638,1991.

articleTitle: Wideband, Polarization-Agile Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: With the ever-increasing demand for high data-rate wireless communications, higher frequency mm-wave bands are becoming more and more lucrative, mainly for the current 5G and the upcoming 6G communication architectures. In an urban environment that comprises buildings, vehicles, trees, etc., lower frequency signals from a transmitting node can get bounced off easily, and enable sufficient signal strength at a non-line-of-sight (NLOS) receiving node by virtue of their longer wavelengths. However, at the mm-wave frequency bands, the corresponding signals will get absorbed and dissipated by the same obstacles due to their very small wavelengths, which can cause a loss of signal at the receiver. As a remedy, the concept of Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RISs) has been gaining popularity lately in the field of wireless communication. These RISs would allow dynamic control of the communication channel by efficiently reflecting/refracting the incoming mm-wave signals while enabling features like gain enhancement, polarization agility, beam steering, and the creation of multiple beams for catering to multiple receiver nodes. Although a relatively new concept in the fields of wireless communication and signal processing, such surfaces have been explored in electromagnetics for a long time, and are commonly known as Reflectarrays (RA) or Transmitarrays (TA), depending on whether the incident beam is being reflected or refracted off of the surface. These surfaces typically comprise numerous periodically arranged resonant-sized or subwavelength conducting structures - known as unit cells - on a flat/conformal surface. The construction of the unit cells determines the operating bandwidth and polarizations supported by the RIS. In order to dynamically control the gain, steering direction, and polarization of the reflected/refracted beam (i.e., to attain reconfigurability), the phases at each of these unit cells need to be controlled, which is typically accomplished by using tunable elements like P-I-N or Varactor diodes, or sometimes RF-MEMS, liquid-crystal or Graphene-based materials that are particularly useful for mm-wave frequencies. These elements can be controlled simply by using an integrated circuit (IC) chip that can regulate the corresponding bias voltages. Lastly, some selective intelligence can be incorporated into the operation of these surfaces by making the output beam either track a moving receiver or by improving the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) at a receiving node in real-time by dynamically controlling the unit cell properties.

articleTitle: Correcting Relative Clock Drift Between Independently-Clocked Antennas Of ALBATROS Radio Telescope Using ORBCOMM Satellites
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Array of Long Baseline Antennas for Taking Radio Observations from Seventy-ninth parallel (ALBATROS) is an under-development interferometric radio telescope that aims to map the sky between 5–30 MHz with few-arcminute resolution-an order-of-magnitude improvement over existing sky-maps in this band. High-resolution maps will allow us to accurately characterize Galactic emission, thus taking the first steps towards detecting cosmic dark ages, and improving our understanding of the astrophysics of the local universe. To minimize contamination from electromagnetic interference of human origin, ALBATROS array is being installed at the Axel Heiberg island (79.8° N, 91.3° W), a radio-quiet location in the Canadian high-Arctic, and has the longest planned baseline of ~20 km to achieve the required resolution. Between 2018 and 2023, ALBATROS operated a 3-antenna array with a maximum baseline of ~3 km at Marion Island (46.9° S, 37.3° E), a radio-quiet location in the sub-Antarctic region. A third, year-round operational array, presently comprising two antennas, has been deployed at Uapishka station (51.5° N, 68.2° W) near Manicouagan reservoir in Quebec, which functions as a testbed for development and reliability testing.

articleTitle: Front End Subsystem Development for a Next Generation Very Large Array
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The ngVLA will provide near-continuous frequency coverage from 1.2 - 116 GHz in multiple bands, with a gap at the atmospheric absorption band between ~50 - 70 GHz. Maximizing sensitivity for each band while also minimizing the overall operating cost are the primary design goals.

articleTitle: First Results from the LIEFSI Campaign - Setup and Calibration
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Electric field double probes are used on many satellite missions to provide high quality in-situ AC and DC electric field measurements. To achieve this accuracy the E-field instrument components and the surrounding surfaces have voltage and current biases applied to them, which mitigate errors due to factors such as the photoelectric effect and stray currents in the system. These measurements are vital for understanding the complex processes that occur in the wide range of plasma environments these satellites orbit through.

articleTitle: Progress Towards Quantum-Enhanced Microwave Remote Sensing and Communication Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: RADAR and communications are vulnerable as noise and interference contaminate the received signals and produce errors limiting their resolution, their accuracy and speed. To answer the growing needs for more reliable and accurate microwave intelligence in an ever more complex electromagnetic environment, there is a growing need to develop innovative microwave sensors with greater signal sensitivity, selectivity and integrity.

articleTitle: Influence of Evaporation Duct Lateral Inhomogeneity on X-Band Propagation
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Evaporation ducts (ED) are an atmospheric phenomenon that can cause inaccuracies in X-band radar systems by enhancing EM energy at ranges beyond the radar horizon. To predict these propagation anomalies, ED characteristics are estimated based-on prevailing meteorological conditions, where these characteristics are commonly assumed to be laterally homogeneous over range, i.e., evaporation duct characteristics don't vary down range from the radar transmitter. While this assumption is reasonable over the open ocean, it commonly breaks down in coastal regions, where it has been shown that the shape of the duct, the strength of the duct (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M-\text{deficit}$</tex>), and/or height of the duct (duct height) is likely to vary over range. Some works have investigated the effects of incorrectly assuming homogeneity and found nonnegligible differences in radar propagation loss predictions (J. Goldhirsh, and D. Dockery, “Propagation Factor Errors Due to the Assumption of Lateral Homogeneity,” Radio Science, vol. 33, issue 2, Mar. 1998). Because of these findings, this work aims to explore under which conditions and to what extent range-dependent variations of the evaporation duct may play a significant factor in accurately predicting radar performance, in-turn exploring the validity and scope of the commonplace lateral homogeneity assumption.

articleTitle: Initial Evaluation of PlanetiQ Grazing GNSS Coherent Reflections for Altimetry Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The exploitation of commercial radio occultations (RO) using Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receiver on SmallSat constellations enable GNSS-Reflectometry (GNSS-R) based all-weather altimetry applications for climate observables at high spatiotemporal resolutions. Utilization of dual-frequency GNSS-R coherent phase observation potentially enables several cm-level geodetic quality altimetric applications. These GNSS bistatic radar phase altimetric measurements could be at low latency, with dense spatially coverage, and capable of synoptic profiling of inland water bodies, sea ice and glaciated surfaces.

articleTitle: Different Geometrical Representations of Partially Reflected Surfaces for Fabry-Perot Antenna Optimization
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A key challenge for designing Fabry-Perot (FP) cavity antennas lies in designing a Partially Reflective Surface (PRS) with high reflection magnitude and a desirable positive phase gradient. This research explores and assesses various PRS unit cell designs for FP cavity antennas: (i) square pixelated, (ii) hexagonal pixelated, (iii) chaos formula, and (iv) super formula configurations. Subsequently, the Genetic Algorithm is utilized to determine the most suitable unit cell for each configuration within the 5 GHz-9 GHz frequency range. The optimization shows that different geometrical representations can yield PRS unit cells with various performances.

articleTitle: Magnetic Anomalies Potentially Attributed to Perseid Bolide Reentry
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: An estimated 50 tons of meteoroidal material rains down upon the earth daily. While most meteors are either largely undetected against a day sky or occur over the vast open oceans or unpopulated areas, hundreds of visual reports of bolides occur daily. While an average meteor releases energy at a rate of tens of gigawatts - equivalent to 10 tons of TNT, as it is disintegrating in the upper atmosphere, large bolides can release energy comparable to nuclear weapons. The 2013 Chelyabinsk bolide released an estimated 550 kilotons TNT equivalent, comparable to about 36 times the yield of the Fat Boy nuclear bomb detonated over Hiroshima. During reentry the kinetic energy of the bolide produces frictional heating, which in turn produces ablation, ionization and fragmentation with concomitant optical radiation. But it has long been claimed that some energy is also emitted in other parts of the electromagnetic spectrum. Researchers have detected ELF and VLF emissions from at least some bolides, but results have been inconsistent across RF frequency and duration, perhaps pointing to the large variation in reentry angle, speed, bolide mass and material composition and likely other factors. A number of causal mechanisms have been proposed for ELF observations during bolide reentries including resonance of the ionized trail and deceleration of electrons and ions within the plasma of the bolide wake or displacement of existing geomagnetic fields through shock wave interactions. We deployed in Northern Virginia a precision three axis induction coil magnetometer sampling at 4000 samples per second from August 14 to August 28, corresponding to the waning end of the Perseid meteor shower. Detections were temporally correlated with optical detection of bolides from the American Meteor Society. We show high correlation between low level magnetic anomalies across the band limited by our sampling rate and optical reports of bolides observed within 200 km. We also note instances were bolides sighted on the West Coast of the U.S. were positively correlated with low level magnetic anomalies sensed in Northern Virginia suggesting sub-ionospherically propagation. While there are many more magnetic anomalies noted than optical bolide reports, we note specific instances where no optical bolides correspond to no sensed magnetic anomalies.

articleTitle: A Practical Superluminal Polarization Current Antenna: Theory, Design, and Construction
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Extended sources of electromagnetic radiation that travel faster than light in vacuo have been built at Los Alamos National Laboratory for more than 15 years. Using accelerated polarization currents as their radiation mechanism, superluminal antennas have been shown to be surprisingly effective emitters of easily steerable, tightly focused beams. In what follows, we describe a superluminal light source whose circular dielectric imparts centripetal acceleration on the moving polarization. Originally designed as a fundamental physics experiment intended to mimic astronomical phenomena, it remains, at least from a science standpoint, the most consequential superluminal emitter constructed to date.

articleTitle: Network-based Design of Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) are an emerging technology for enhancing the capability and performance of 5G and 6G mobile communications (Y. Liu et al., in IEEE Commun. Surv. Tutor, vol. 23, no. 3, pp. 1546-1577,2021). A RIS can be designed to electronically control the shape and direction of reflected or transmitted electromagnetic waves. Application scenarios generally involve mounting RISs on buildings to create a virtual-line-of-sight between users to improve wireless coverage. In this work, we propose a RIS topology and introduce an approach for designing it. The proposed RIS is shown in Fig. 1 (J. Loncar, A. Grbic, and S. Hrabar, in IEEE Trans. Antennas Propag, vol. 66, no. 6, pp. 3213–3218, 2018). It consists of N×N cells, where each cell is connected to a port. The RIS has four different layers: a patch layer, a slotted ground plane layer, a microstrip line layer with ports, and finally a hidden network layer which can have reactive loads and interconnecting networks that are connected to the ports. Each cell is designed to match a broadside incident field to a 50 Ohm microstrip line.

articleTitle: Scaling Laws for Solid-State Opening Switch Generators
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The introduction of powerful nanosecond opening switches in the form of the Drift Step Recovery Diode (DSRD) and the Semiconductor Opening Switch (SOS) have enabled MW-GW class solid-state modulators with repetition rates extending into the MHz regime. These switches take advantage of an intermediate inductive storage stage that shunts the current of a resonant circuit to the load. The nature of these switches relies on driving currents in order to realize the nanosecond current cutoff effect in the base regions of the device, which ties the device performance to the driving circuit. An intuitive understanding of the key tradeoffs in the circuit design require a simplified model of the current cutoff effect and overall interaction with the circuit. Focusing on the DSRD, a simplified model of the interruption process is tied to circuit characteristics to look at important metrics for pulser design. Voltage gain, rise time, and efficiency are solved for depending on circuit impedance, pumping times for an arbitrary stack of DSRD diodes.

articleTitle: Photonic-Integrated Modulators as Millimeter and Submillimeter-Wave Hyperspectral Receivers with no Pre-Amplification
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Advances in remote sensing instrumentation have been critical for the improvement of climate models and numerical weather predictions. Different meteorological variables such as temperature, water vapor, ice content, precipitation, etc., can be measured from satellites by using passive or active (radar) microwave sensors observing at specific frequency bands ranging from several GHz to about 900 GHz. These receivers must exhibit sufficiently low noise figures to provide accurate measurements in relatively short integration times. Moreover, high spectral resolution (tens of MHz) is often critical for the retrieval of the atmospheric metrics of interest. Despite only power measurements being needed, heterodyne receiver frontends followed by intermediate frequency (IF) digitization backends are usually implemented to provide the desired spectral resolution. Although the multiple frequency bands of interest are relatively narrow, they are often scattered over several GHz, for which the backends incorporate bulky filter stages to split the IF signal into multiple narrowband channels that accommodate the limited sampling rate of the ADCs.

articleTitle: RFI Issues for the Next Generation Very Large Array (ngVLA)
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Building on the remarkable success of the VLA, VLBA, and ALMA, NRAO is planning a large collecting area interferometer which will replace the VLA and VLBA - the next generation Very Large Array (ngVLA) [1]. For many of the same reasons that the VLA was constructed where it was (fraction of sky visible, quality of site, accessibility, etc.), the core and bulk of the collecting area of the ngVLA will be on the Plains of San Agustin, near where the center of the current VLA is. Despite the general quality of the site, RFI is nearly ubiquitous, especially at frequencies below 2 GHz, and the spectrum is getting worse with time, as experienced in other areas across the world. Also, because of the spatial resolution needed to satisfy science requirements, antennas will be spread across the U.S., Canada, and northern Mexico, and so be in different RFI environments (see Figure 1 for locations of antennas in the current design) [2], [3].

articleTitle: Multi-Dimensional Image Completion for Automated Power Amplifier Design
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Widely used methods to characterize maximum power, efficiency, or linear performance for power amplifiers require many iterative impedance measurements. This cumbersome process has been simplified by applying a Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network (WGAN) Image Completion network trained for load-pull extrapolation (A. Egbert, C. Baylis, and R. J. Marks, “Extrapolation of Load-Pull Data: A Novel Use of GAN Artificial Intelligence Image Completion,” IEEE Transactions on Microwave Theory and Techniques, vol. 70, no. 11, pp. 4849–4856, Nov. 2022). In this work, randomly generated linear S-parameters were used to train a model that could predict the load reflection coefficients for both linear and nonlinear devices with a median optimal error below 0.1. The Smith Chart can be extended into a 3<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">rd</sup> dimension and is called a Smith Tube, which can be used to illustrate device characteristics' dependencies on additional design variables aside from impedance. This presentation considers possible approaches and expected challenges of extending this work to multidimensional characterization using the Smith Tube.

articleTitle: Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Using a Uniform Linear Array Considering Antenna Radiation Patterns
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A UHF antenna array is proposed for direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimations. In conventional direction finding (DF) systems, it is assumed that antenna elements have isotropic patterns and mutual coupling among these elements are neglected, leading to compromised DF accuracies. In this work, complex radiation patterns with the presence of mutual coupling among antenna elements are simultaneously considered through full-wave numerical simulations of the antenna array. The antenna patterns rather than simplified array factors are applied in DF algorithms. Both Cramer-Rao bound (CRB) calculations and multiple signal classification (MUSIC) algorithm are implemented to validate the DF performance of the UHF antenna array.

articleTitle: Spectral Calibration of the Electrojet Zeeman Imaging Explorer – Microwave Electrojet Magnetogram Polarimetric Radiometer System
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Electrojet Zeeman Imaging Explorer (EZIE) mission is a NASA Heliophysics Explorer mission led by APL-John Hopkins, with NASA-JPL and Blue Canyon Technologies as partners. EZIE is responsible for measuring auroral electrojet and the induced magnetic field vector in the Earth's ionosphere through the MEM (Microwave Electrojet Magnetogram) radiometer system. EZIE will help explain key interactions between the Earth's upper atmosphere, ionosphere, and the surrounding space.

articleTitle: Incoherent Scattering from an Object Above a Rough Surface
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: An analytical second order solution for the ensemble average incoherent scattering from an object above a rough surface is presented. The four-path model is applied as a first order scattering approximation used to decouple the scattering from the surface and the object. The Kirchhoff integral and the small slope approximation are also applied to quantify scattering from the rough surface. Under these assumptions, the mean radar cross section can be expressed in terms of first, second, third, and fourth order interactions in relation to the rough surface. This presentation focuses on the derivation and evaluation of the first and second order contributions.

articleTitle: Improving a Machine Learning Model for Satellite Precipitation Downscaling
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Precipitation products at high space and time resolutions are critical for applications such as flood monitoring and water resources management. However, the space resolutions of commonly used satellite precipitation products, such as the NASA Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement (IMERG, 10-km resolution) and NOAA/Climate Prediction Center morphing technique (CMORPH, 8-km resolution), are not sufficient for such applications. We have developed a generative adversarial network (GANs) based model, PrecipSRGAN, to create a super-resolution version of CMORPH, which has a spatial resolution of 4 km by 4 km. The super-resolution model uses the Stage IV quantitative precipitation estimates (QPEs) as references and takes advantage of the digital elevation model (DEM) to improve satellite-based precipitation feature extraction. Independent precipitation events were selected to evaluate the model performance. In addition, the deep learning-based downscaling performance was compared with a linear interpolation method. Based on the testing events and ground references, the PrecipSRGAN outperforms the linear interpolation-based satellite precipitation product given evaluation methods such as correlation (CC), normalized mean error (NME), etc. However, after comparing the deep learning-based downscaling product with the ground-truth dataset, it was noticed that the model inherits a terraindependent bias from the original CMORPH precipitation retrieval product that tends to overestimate precipitation in the Central Valley and underestimate precipitation over the mountainous regions, such as the Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada. Therefore, this study attempts to improve the downscaling performance by adding weight factors to the loss function. The goal of such a weight matrix is to assign varying weights to the data points based on their precipitation levels. So that to give heavier penalty to the light rainy points and lighter penalty to the heavy rainy points. Testing results have demonstrated enhanced performance based on this adaption.

articleTitle: An In Situ Characterization of 1.7 GHz Building Entry Loss
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In this manuscript, we assess the suitability of the ITU Recommendation P.2109 building entry loss models through continuous-wave and broadband measurements conducted in two distinct buildings: a historical structure and a recently constructed modern building. The findings reveal that both the construction material type and the density of materials significantly influence the entry loss. Moreover, our results indicate that the P.2109 categories of “traditional” and “thermally efficient” might not adequately describe the intricacies of building construction, leading to challenges in accurately inferring propagation loss values.

articleTitle: Link Budget Analysis of Interrogation of Surface Acoustic Wave Sensors in Metallic Tubular Structures
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In this paper, we report on loss mechanisms contributing to the link budget for interrogation of Surface Acoustic Wave (SAW) devices in metallic tubular structures. Impedance matching losses associated with a SAW device are minimized by design optimization and antenna coupling losses and resulting propagation losses are measured in metallic tubular structures enabling prediction of interrogation distances with various antenna configurations.

articleTitle: Singular Metric for Antenna Array Mutual Coupling: Unveiling the Array Coupling Index (ACI)
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In this paper, we present a novel approach for quantifying mutual coupling within antenna arrays. Our method introduces a unified metric, referred to as the Array Coupling Index (ACI), which succinctly captures the collective mutual coupling effect among array elements. The formulation reveals that mutual coupling is intricately linked to impedance matching and provides insight into the worst-case coupling scenario within a specific array configuration. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we analyze several illustrative examples, showcasing the effectiveness of our method in characterizing and understanding mutual coupling phenomena within antenna arrays.

articleTitle: Spatial Imaging and Zonal Drift Motion Tracking of Equatorial Plasma Bubbles over South America Using Specially Detrended GPS TEC Data
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In this work, we explored some potentially new applications of global navigation satellite system (GNSS) total electron content (TEC) data from South America for characterizing the morphology and physical properties of equatorial plasma bubbles (EPBs). Here we used global positioning system (GPS) TEC observations that had been detrended using a special numerical technique (R. Pradipta, C. E. Valladares, and P. H. Doherty, “An effective TEC data detrending method for the study of equatorial plasma bubbles and traveling ionospheric disturbances”, J. Geophys. Res. Space Physics, vol. 120, issue 12, 2015). This special GPS TEC data detrending technique utilizes a mechanical analogy of a rolling barrel on a rough terrain, which allows it to deduce a suitable baseline from the TEC observations. Through this GPS TEC data detrending method, the net ΔTEC (= original TEC minus the baseline TEC) would show both the depletions associated with EPBs and the oscillations associated with traveling ionospheric disturbances (TIDs). The ΔTEC values along individual ionospheric piercing points (IPPs) were interpolated into a uniform rectangular geographic latitude and longitude grid with 0.2°x0.2° spatial resolution, covering the South American sector, and with a 3-minute time resolution between consecutive maps. For this study, GPS TEC observation data from the year 2011 were used.

articleTitle: Removing Clock-Drift and Ionospheric Errors from the CHIME-KKO VLBI Delays
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment Fast Radio Burst project (CHIME/FRB) and its three outrigger telescopes will form a Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) network, with the goal of localising many hundreds of one-off and repeating FRBs to sub-arcsecond precision. Phase calibration is essential for successful VLBI, and requires removing errors due to ionosphere, clock, and instrumental delays. For calibrating the VLBI network, we plan to employ pulsars and traditional steady radio sources spread over the entire sky as calibrators. The first CHIME/FRB Outrigger, k'niʔatn k'l‿stk'masqt (KKO), came online in June 2022 and has been in commissioning ever since. It has a 66-km line of sight distance to CHIME and can provide a localisation accuracy of 1 arcsecond along the direction of the baseline. As the pathfinder for the outriggers, KKO has enabled the development and testing of our VLBI calibration techniques.

articleTitle: A Distributed Array of Low-Cost GNSS-Based Sensors for Monitoring and Studies of Mid-Latitude Ionospheric Irregularities and Scintillation
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We have devoted efforts to the development and deployment of a new low-cost ionospheric sensor over mid-latitudes (Rodrigues and Moraes, 2019; Gomez Socola and Rodrigues, 2022). The latest version of this sensor is called ScintPi3.0 and is capable of measuring L-band ionospheric scintillation and Total Electron Content (TEC) at a high rate. The study of ionospheric irregularities and scintillations is important because they affect radio-communications and radio navigation systems such as the Global Position System (GPS).

articleTitle: Arcsecond localizations with the first CHIME-Outriggers Telescope
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME) telescope is a phased array interferometer operating across the 400–800 MHz band whose wide field of view has allowed for the detection of thousands of fast radio bursts (FRBs). Currently, the CHIME/FRB Outriggers project is constructing a VLBI network with three identical outrigger telescopes with the goal of localizing a large sample of one-off FRBs to their host galaxies. Achieving these science goals requires solving numerous calibration challenges unique to CHIME Outriggers. For instance, while phase referencing to bright, compact calibrators is a common VLBI practice to remove atmospheric effects and differential dispersive delays from the ionosphere, little is known about compact source populations at CHIME/Outrigger frequencies and baselines.

articleTitle: Heterogeneous Integration of Biasing Circuits for mmWave Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We present the design of a biasing circuit and interposer architecture for scalable millimeter wave (mmWave) reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs). Specifically, a multilayer biasing board is designed to provide the necessary excitation of a 1-bit RIS. Ball grid array (BGA) technology is leveraged to integrate heterogeneous technologies and materials to provide more real estate on the RIS metasurface and more design flexibility. Fabrication and assembly challenges associated with this novel technique have been identified and recommendations for future fabrication/assembly are provided.

articleTitle: Cyclostationary Channel Power Measurements for CBRS Coexistence Assessment
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: We present a compressive approach for channel power measurements in coexistence scenarios involving heteroge-neous cyclostationary channel usage and an example application in the Citizens Broadband Radio Service (CBRS) band. The method leverages known cycle periods of anticipated spectrum users, including wireless data networks with time-division duplexing and pulsed radar, to analyze channel power within a cyclic analysis period. The high degree of data reduction and low degree of computational complexity makes this method suitable for edge computing and long-term spectrum monitoring applications. The results of applying this technique to data recorded in the CBRS band demonstrate its effectiveness in distinguishing signal types, enabling coexistence assessment and supporting data-driven management of spectrum sharing frameworks.

articleTitle: Amplified THz Detection in p-Diamond TeraFET Induced by Fixed Drain Current
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper explores the amplification of continuous wave terahertz (THz) detection in p-diamond TeraFET using constant DC current bias and investigates the influence of a constant DC current supply on resonant response. Results indicate that a low drift velocity below the instability threshold enhances THz resonant detection, amplifying signals. Conversely, high drift velocities exceeding the threshold limit eliminate resonant response, as instability dominates. The latter region behaves more like a broadband detection.

articleTitle: Liquid-Metal-Based Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A typical reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) consists of an array of unit cells, each containing a few unconnected conducting segments. Reconfiguration of the array, and thus its reflective properties, is usually achieved using varactor or PIN diodes serving as switches to connect/disconnect the otherwise isolated conducting segments. This results in a different geometry for each unit cell, which can then be patterned in a way to create a phase gradient across the array surface, resulting in redirection of an incident electromagnetic wave in a specified direction.

articleTitle: SAFARI - A Differential Approach to Probe the Cosmological Sky-Averaged 21-cm Signal
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In contrast to large radio interferometric arrays, by using a single broadband antenna or a small compact array, sky-averaged (global) 21-cm experiments offer a complementary and experimentally simpler means to measure the highly redshifted cosmological neutral hydrogen spin-flip 21-cm transition for studying the thermal and ionization evolution of the intergalactic medium (IGM) in the early Universe (~ 400,000 after the Big Bang). Two main challenges in separating the weak cosmological 21-cm signal from galactic and extragalatic synchrotron emission are the limited knowledge of the absolute foreground sky brightness below ~ 400 MHz, and the uncertain frequency-dependent (chromatic) antenna beam response. Although the former is typically parametrized by a spectrally smooth power law function, it is highly unconstrained due to incomplete spectral and spatial coverage by existing sky survey maps. Meanwhile, intrinsic beam chromaticity of a broadband antenna distorts the foreground spectrum and further complicates the differentiation of the underlying global 21-cm spectrum. There is no accurate means to characterize the in situ antenna beam pattern to the required level at those frequencies besides limited success from joint constraint of antenna range measurement and computational electromagnetics (CEM) simulation. As an attempt to overcome these two obstacles, we propose a differential measurement concept, the Scaled Antennas For Ascertaining the Radio Index (SAFARI), which utilizes a series of electromagnetically scaled, narrow-band, high gain corner-reflector antennas to sample the sky spectrum around discrete frequencies between 40-180 MHz with near-identical in situ beam patterns. In this talk, I will illustrate, through simulations, that by empirically computing the spectral index as the logarithmic differentiation between sky measurements made at two adjacent frequencies, the observed spectral index can used as a proxy to probe the background global 21-cm signal. The conceptual instrument design, error analysis, deployment strategy, and engineering challenges for the SAFARI prototype will be summarized.

articleTitle: Instability Variability Characteristics Derived from Beacon Satellite Observations
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Spread F is probably the most well-known phenomenon in the ionospheric community. The broad spectrum of density irregularities associated with the causal Rayleigh-Taylor instability generates a wide range of radio signals spanning the HF through UHF frequency bands. Longitudinal differences in seasonal activity patterns, largely explained by the relationship between the local magnetic field geometry and the solar terminator orientation, have been well established through a combination of ground- and space-based observations over the last three decades. More recently, an analysis of daily spread F occurrence as determined by low latitude VHF and GNSS scintillation activity shows results that are statistically consistent with previously established climatologies, but the level of day-to-day variability in the occurrence data show marked variations with longitude and solar flux. Specifically, the American sector shows very low in-season variability for F10.7 values exceeding a relatively moderate value of about 130 sfu, while the African and Asian sectors exhibit true day-to-day variability regardless of seasonal variations or solar flux levels within the limits of the observations. These intriguing results are not fully understood yet, but the implications are clear: at least in limited longitude windows, seasonal factors control the occurrence of spread F irregularities with little variability; gravity waves or other “seeds” appear to play no significant role. Moreover, the physical parameters believed to control the Rayleigh-Taylor instability-field-line integrated <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E$</tex> & <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$F$</tex> region conductivities, electric field, thermospheric winds, collision rate and vertical electron density gradient-must not all be relevant or at least truly variable; that is, some parameters are playing a more important role or are robust with respect to daily variability. Using a physics-based low latitude spread F model, we assess the primary drivers controlling occurrence as a function of longitude. The results have significant implications for space weather as they suggest that meaningful long-term forecasts of equatorial scintillation may be possible within specific longitude boundaries. And importantly, although day-to-day variability is higher at other longitudes, it is reasonable to believe that some parameters are more critical than others in determining instability occurrence even in those regions. These result were facilitated by beacon satellite measurements and would not have been possible with space-based in situ observations alone.
