articleTitle: An Analysis of Low-Cost SDRs to Meet City-Wide Spectrum Utilization Measurement Requirements
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper surveys the current marketplace offerings for low-cost software-defined radio (SDR) technology and proposes a framework for cost-optimizing distributed sensing networks using a scenario in the Citizens Broadband Radio Service band. To determine which SDR to select, it is necessary to model sensor performance within its operating context. We identify detection radius as a metric of primary concern in cost-optimizing a sensor network, and determine that further work is required to evaluate the sensitivity of low-cost SDRs.

articleTitle: Superconducting Kinetic Inductance-Based On-Chip Frequency Conversion
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In addition to the standard geometric inductance, superconductors have a kinetic inductance that can have a strong quadratic dependence on current. We use this nonlinearity to generate large harmonics of GHz signals by etching a 0.5 m long meandered coplanar waveguide from a 60 nm thick NbTiN sputtered film. After cooling the fabricated chip to 3 K, we measure a maximum on-chip conversion efficiency from 10 GHz to 20 GHz of 14% when applying a 2.5 dBm 10 GHz signal and a 20 rnA dc current bias. The measured powers up to the third harmonic and changes in phase agree with harmonic balance simulations of the nonlinear system. We anticipate that further optimization of the design including frequency dispersion engineering will significantly increase the conversion efficiency. This approach and material, which has a critical temperature above 15K, is also extendable up to THz frequencies; we chose to operate at 10s of GHz based on the available instruments and cabling.

articleTitle: Updates on the Optics Design of the ngVLA 18-meter Reflector System
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The next generation Very Large Array (ngVLA) will consist of shaped offset Gregorian dual reflector antennas with approximately 244 antennas with an 18-meter aperture diameter and 19 antennas with 6-meter aperture diameter. At the reflector system's focus is a suite of cryogenic feeds which cover the frequency range from 1.2 GHz to 116 GHz with a gap at the atmospheric absorption band between 50.5 GHz and 70 GHz. The first 18-meter prototype antenna will be assembled at the VLA site early in 2024.

articleTitle: Direct-RF Full Duplex Radio With 22-dB/200-MHz Digital Self-Interference Cancellation
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper presents a new full-duplex transceiver exhibiting wideband digital self-interference cancellation (DSIC). To achieve strong cancellation, a direct-RF sampling architecture is employed to significantly reduce the number of analog components in the transceiver chain. The entire transceiver is realized using a single field programmable gate array (FPGA) as part of a radio-frequency system-on-chip (RFSoC) development kit. This RFSoC integrates RF-sampling data converters, i.e., digital-to-analog converter (RF-DAC) and analog-to-digital converter (RF-ADC) along with the FPGA fabric on the same chip. The employed 5G OFDM waveform is synthesized on the XCZU28DR chip as part of the transceiver's testbed. The efficacy of the proposed transceiver and the canceller algorithm is demonstrated using SI cancellation ratio (SICR) level. Hardware measurements demonstrated 22 dB of digital cancellation across a modulation bandwidth of 200 MHz. To the best of the author's knowledge, this is the first-ever demonstration of a wideband radio self-interference cancellation at the digital back-end.

articleTitle: Effects of Mismatch Between Digital Elevation Models and Numerical Weather Prediction Terrain Heights on Propagation Modeling
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The US Navy is increasingly operating in littoral regions, and the Marine Corps has historically operated in inland regions. Because of this, interest is increasing in applying models that have traditionally been used in oceanic regions to inland areas. While semi-empirical models such as Irregular Terrain Model (ITM) and Terrain Integrated Rough Earth Model (TIREM) have been used to model radio frequency (RF) electromagnetic (EM) wave propagation over land for decades, these models do not deterministically model atmospheric effects. The Navy typically uses Parabolic Equation (PE) models such as Tropospheric Electromagnetic Parabolic Equation Routine (TEMPER) to model RF EM propagation because these models deterministically account for atmospheric conditions by ingesting refractivity profiles. PE models are preferred over semi-empirical models in oceanic environments because of the prevalence of anomalous propagation, which necessitates accurate atmospheric characterization.

articleTitle: Profiling and Optimizing the High Performance Gridder
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Radio interferometric imaging with current and future instruments requires the handling of large datasets. GPUs provide an effective means of dealing with this data deluge. However, to fully leverage the computational power available on these GPUs, a tightly coupled iterative approach involving performance engineering and software engineering is required.

articleTitle: Statistics of LF-MF Auroral Radio Emissions Observed at South Pole Station in 2020
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In 2022–2023, Dartmouth College in collaboration with University of New Brunswick set up receiving systems to measure natural auroral radio emissions at three sites in Nunavut, Canada: Qikiktarjuaq, Iqaluit, and Halls Beach. These sites surround the point which is geomagnetically conjugate to South Pole Station, Antarctica, where a similar radio recieving system operates. Multiple examples have bee recorded of simultaneous radio emissions at South Pole Station and one of the northern hemisphere sites, including both LF auroral hiss and 2fce and 3fce cyclotron harmonic emissions. About half of the conjugate LF auroral hiss events occurred within one month of equinox. In two examples near solstices, the hiss in the sunlit hemisphere is much weaker than that in the dark hemisphere. In about half of the examples, the LF hiss initiates at the same time in the two hemispheres to within 10 seconds. In most of the other cases, hiss occurs first in one hemisphere or the other by 100–200 seconds. The initial data show no obvious relationship between IMF conditions and simultaneity or lack thereof of the LF hiss in the two hemispheres. Near equinox multiple examples of simultaneous 2fce cyclotron harmonic emissions have been recorded, but away from equinox conditions, observation of 2fce in the dark hemisphere simultaneous with 3fce in the daylit hemisphere is more common, as expected because the higher density in the daylit hemisphere favors emission of higher harmonics. A surprising result of these observations is that on occasion the structure and frequency dispersion of the cyclotron harmonic emissions in the two hemispheres are similar, suggesting that local conditions may not be as dominant in determining the fine structure of the emissions as previously thought.

articleTitle: Guiding of the Whistler-Mode Waves by the Localized Depletions of the Magnetic Field
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This study explores the behavior of extremely-low frequency (ELF) whistler-mode waves in small-scale magnetic field depletions known as Low-magnetic ducts (LBD) within Earth's magnetosphere. The main focus is on demonstrating that LBDs allow electromagnetic energy to escape outside the duct.

articleTitle: Observing More Equatorial Irregularity Physics Using GNSS Scintillation Parameters
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: It is common to use L-band GNSS amplitude scintillation to track the statistical occurrence of turbulent fluctuations in the ionosphere near the Fresnel scale (a distance-dependent 300–500 m scale transverse to the ray propagation path). The amplitude scintillation index, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{S}_{4}$</tex>, has the advantage of responding to the integrated turbulent strength, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{k}}\mathrm{L}$</tex>, while being mostly insensitive to net ionospheric drift and large-scale TEC structures. In this talk, we explore the relationship of the GNSS <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{S}_{4}$</tex> parameter to the integrated strength of turbulence with examples of how it can provide additional information on the ionospheric state-e.g., whether recent development or decaying irregularities-during equatorial plasma bubble (EPB) observations. However, it is useful and important to augment <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{S}_{4}$</tex> with the power law spectral index (p) and the decorrelation time <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\tau)$</tex>. Multi-band <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{S}_{4}$</tex> measurements (e.g., L1 and L5) can further extend the lower-end range of sensitivity, which is typically limited by receiver thermal noise, to lower <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{k}}\mathrm{L}$</tex> values than can be observed by L1 measurements alone. All of these measurements can be facilitated by modern commercial GNSS receivers capable of recording high-rate time series data, some of which are inexpensive (under US$550 in cost).

articleTitle: Electromagnetic Uncertainty Analysis of 3D Biological Phantoms
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Cellphone and other wireless device electromagnetic (EM) radiation assessments are needed to approve the use of those devices near human bodies. Approval of such devices near a human body requires them to meet power deposition/specific absorption rate (SAR) standards. Current standards and guidelines do not account for variations in tissue properties and size. Most electromagnetic analyses of biological models are performed using the finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) method [Tafllove et al.]. Variations in tissue properties and size may be accounted for in these models using uncertainty analysis. Monte Carlo FDTD (MC FDTD) is one such method that requires numerous FDTD runs based on variational statistics to provide mean and standard deviation SAR metrics. For uncertainty analysis, the MC method is considered the gold standard even though it is computationally very expensive.

articleTitle: Second-Order Exceptional Point of Degeneracy in Two Directly Coupled Resonator
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: An exceptional point of degeneracy (EPD) occurs when two or more eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenvectors coalesce. In the past, EPDs in coupled resonators have been obtained using PT-symmetric circuits. Furthermore, EPDs have been demonstrated in a time-varying single LC resonator, and in two resonators coupled via a gyrator (K. Rouhi, A. Nikzamir, A. Figotin, and F. Capolino, “Exceptional point in a degenerate system made of a gyrator and two unstable resonators,” Physical Review A, vol. 105, no. 3, 2022) that do not require loss or gain components. Here, we present another way to achieve an EPD using two connected Foster and non-Foster resonators. Non-Foster networks are networks with one or more non-F oster components. In non-Foster components the derivative of reactance or susceptance is zero or negative. As a consequence, networks with negative inductance or capacitance are essentially non-Foster networks. A negative component can be realized using an operational amplifier in an inverter circuit.

articleTitle: Exploiting Dense Coherent Reflection Track Areas in the Indonesian Seas to Investigate the Performance of Spire GNSS-R Ocean Altimetry
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Spaceborne GNSS reflectometry (GNSS-R) precision ocean altimetry has been demonstrated to decimeter levels using carrier-phase observations from grazing-angle ocean reflections received on several low-Earth orbit (LEO) platforms including the Cyclone GNSS and Spire Global constellations in areas of high coherence such as quiet waters. In the open ocean, calm surface conditions are mainly found in the Gulf of Mexico and Indonesian Seas. Our study in the Gulf of Mexico showed that the grazing-angle Spire phase data can detect the large sea-level signature of the strong Loop-Current for moderate specular point elevations. However, almost half of these coherent Spire tracks provided retrievals inconsistent with the gridded sea level anomaly (SLA) derived from multi-mission nadir radar altimeters. We suspect that instrumental, atmospheric and/or geophysical correction errors either mismodelled or unaccounted for in our Spire's altimetry retrievals are the cause of the mismatch.

articleTitle: A Compact Single-Bit Dual-Pol Unit Cell Design for mmWave Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Except for the sub-6GHz bands, 5G and future generations of wireless communications rely on millimeter wave (mmWave) frequencies to achieve higher data rates, extend broadband internet to a larger portion of the population, and potentially achieve new promising applications and services that combine the synergy or sensing and communications. However, the effort to achieve practical coverage of mmWave signals stumbles on the unfavorable propagation characteristics of higher frequency EM waves. Mmwaves cover much shorter distances than the sub-6GHz signals due to absorption and/or strong scattering from most materials in a typical communication channel. As such, it is very common for the user equipment (UE) to receive unacceptably low signal-to-noise (SNR) signals or experience no coverage at all. Densifying the base station (BS) network is an approach that will improve signal coverage, this comes at a substantial capital expenditure due to the costs associated with the hardware, installation, and maintenance of such complicated systems. Alternatively, using active repeaters or passive reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) are potential solutions to the mmWave coverage challenges.

articleTitle: Superconducting Integrated Filters for Kinetic-Inductance Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifiers
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The sky contains plenty of information about star formation, galaxy evolution and the cosmic microwave background at microwaves and millimeter waves. Most astronomical observations require coherent amplification of weak signals from the sky to enable readout. Superconducting kinetic-inductance traveling-wave parametric amplifiers (KI - TWP As) have demonstrated quantum-limited noise performance across over-an-octave bandwidths. At the same time, the semiconductor low-noise amplifiers (LNAs) are necessary as subsequent amplification stages to bring the readout signals amplitudes to usable levels.

articleTitle: A Novel Shaped Symmetric Wideband Dielectric Resonator Antenna by Binary Material Optimization
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to design Wideband Dielectric Resonator Antennas (DRA) with distinctive shape by leveraging binary material optimization. In this method, a traditional solid bulk DRA structure was partitioned into multiple smaller blocks, each assigned with a unique permittivity variable. This allocation was carefully orchestrated to ensure a symmetrical material distribution within the resonator. A genetic algorithm was employed to optimize the material profile, leading to the creation of a newly shaped DRA. The proposed design yields an impressive 104% fractional bandwidth covering the frequency range from 4.54 to 14.41 GHz at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$S_{11}=- 10 dB$</tex> with peak gain of 5.1 dB. This bandwidth represents a significant improvement over the original bulk DRA design, Showcasing the effectiveness and potential of the binary material optimization technique in enhancing antenna performance.

articleTitle: MIMO WiFi Imaging Based on Reconfigurable Passive EM Skins
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The integration of Reconfigurable Passive Electro-magnetic (EM) skins in WiFi-based Imaging systems offers a smart and cost-effective improvement of achievable resolution. The research about smart displacement of properly designed RISs has already proved the capability to overcome the spatial resolution limitations given by off-the-shelf WiFi systems. This article looks into a RIS-aided WIFi imaging system based on MIMO antennas for achieving high-resolution results. After drafting a valuable beamforming model to account for RIS presence, we discuss about the performance carried out by a MIMO based RX-TX compared to single-antenna case. This investigation takes also into account the modeling of different phase contributions provided by the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M$</tex> × <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N$</tex> single cells displaced over the passive surface. Particular attention will be given to the finite phase quantization, negatively impacting over imaging resolution.

articleTitle: Appraisal of the Rice-Squared Model for Scattering Fiom an Object Above a Sea Surface
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Rice-Squared probability density function (PDF) is widely-accepted model by radar engineers for describing the statistics of the backscattered field of an object located above a rough sea surface. This model is roughly justified via the premise that the statistics of the amplitude of the field impinging on the object in the presence of the sea surface can be closely described by a Rician PDF. A sloppy application of the reciprocity theorem leads people to conclude that the amplitude of the backscattered field has a Rice-Squared PDF. In this paper we carefully examine the application of the reciprocity theorem to the problem of backscatter from an object over a rough sea surface and rigorously show that the Rice-Squared model is strictly applicable to point targets above sea surface. We also present backscatter statistics of an extended object located above sea surface, which are calculated via a physics-based model.

articleTitle: White Rabbit: Precision Time and Frequency Distribution for PANOSETI and High-Speed Data Transportation Between NIC and GPU Over 400G Network
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: White rabbit is an open-source system for time and frequency distribution over Ethernet and is used in radio and optical astronomy, as well as physics and other radio applications. Users can purchase commercial off-the-shelf white rabbit switches, or integrate white rabbit circuitry into custom boards, with parts costing about $40 per node. White Rabbit achieves a 1 PPS time accuracy better than 30ns RMS, using 1 Gbit/sec Ethernet over optical fiber. Time accuracy and precision is stable and largely independent of temperature and fiber length because White Rabbit measures and compensates for the delay from different lengths of fibers automatically.

articleTitle: Satellite and Space Debris Identification by Measurements of Ionospheric Interactions
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Space objects traveling through the ionosphere launch both electrostatic and electromagnetic waves that may used for tracking of space debris. In addition, satellites that fire chemical or ion thrusters can produce easily detectable optical or plasma wave disturbances.

articleTitle: GNSS Signals of Opportunity Synthetic Aperture Radar Concept for High Resolution Imaging of Terrain Surfaces
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: High resolution (~100m) remote sensing of Soil Moisture (SM) and Vegetation Water Content (VWC) is critical for investigations of land surface hydrological and ecological processes along with applications to water resource management, agriculture yield, flood prediction and weather forecasts. Due to their importance, L-band (~1 GHz) microwave passive microwave missions, including the ESA Soil Moisture and Ocean Salinity (SMOS) and NASA Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) missions with a swath width of 1000 km have been providing these two observables from space with a global coverage of every 2–3 days, however at a coarse resolution of about 30 km. In contrast the L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) missions, such as the Japanese PALSAR-series and future NASA-ISRO SAR (NISAR), can provide high resolution, but with a narrower swath of about 250 km, limiting the temporal revisit of 6 to 12 days. To achieve a temporal revisit of 1–3 days with the nominal active SAR technologies, like PALSAR or NISAR, will require a constellation of satellites, which will require a high implementation cost. The Signals-of-Opportunity (SoOp) reflectometry, which is the basis of the NASA CYGNSS mission, can provide low-cost passive radar observations of earth surfaces, however with a limited spatial resolution of mostly about 20 km and no swath coverage. To address the scientific needs with an affordable cost, we have investigated the design of L-band GNSS-based SoOp SAR for high resolution and frequent coverage from space. The design employs an electronic scanning antenna to enable the tracking of reflections of multiple GNSS satellites, which can possibly allow an effective total swath of 1000 km or greater, and thus a temporal revisit of better than 3 days and a high spatial resolution. We have completed a signal to noise ratio (SNR) analysis. The SNR analysis is based on the SoOpSAR design equations (S. Yueh R. Shah X. Xu, B. Stiles, and X. Bosch-Lluis, “A Satellite Synthetic Aperture Radar Concept Using P-Band Signals of Opportunity,” IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Applied Earth Observations and Remote Sensing, Vol. 28, Feb 2021), which require the values of normalized bistatic radar cross sections (NBRCS) of land surfaces near the specular direction. According to the CYGNSS NBRCS data and theoretical estimation based the Kirchhoff scattering model for scattering off the azimuth from the specular point, the range of NBRCS is mostly in the range of 10 to 40 dB. With the NBRCS of 10 dB, 32 dBW for the Equivalent Isotropically Radiated Power (EIRP) of GNSS satellites, and a receiver antenna gain of 30 dB, a positive SNR can be achieved with a swath of 200 km for a low earth orbit altitude of 600 km. The antenna beamwidth for an antenna aperture of 2 m for the antenna gain of 30 dB is about 6 degrees, which can enable a dwell time of greater than 10 seconds, and therefore a resolution of about 2 m on the ground by Doppler filtering. The range resolution for a bandwidth of 10 MHz will vary across track. We will present the design of the GNSS-SoOpSAR along with conceptual extension to use multiple satellites to achieve single-pass interferometric SAR processing for detection of surface elevation and 3-D mapping by tomography.

articleTitle: Comparison of Different Microwave Tissue Phantoms for the Design of an Optimal Validation System for RF Devices
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Biosensing is a technique used to examine an individual's internal anatomy without the need for invasive surgery. There are many modalities used for biosensing, but the unifying factor for each is their ability to differentiate between abnormal and healthy tissue through differences in the tissue's material properties. Among them, biosensing through the propagation of electromagnetic waves in the radiofrequency (RF) and microwave spectral regions has proven to be more effective due to its unique properties. The most ideal way to test microwave systems for biosensing is through excised tissue, however, there are health and ethical concerns related to obtaining excised tissue. As a result, tissue mimicking materials, which are also known as tissue phantoms, are a necessary tool that can be used to test microwave propagation through biological tissue. Tissue phantoms are inorganic materials that replicate the properties of biological tissue. According to the article, (S. Castello-Palacios, C. Garcia-Pardo, M. Alloza-Pascual, A. Fornes-Leal, N. Cardona and A. Valles-Lluch, “Gel Phantoms for Body Microwave Propagation in the (2 to 26.5) GHz Frequency Band,” IEEE Transactions on Atennas and Propagation, pp. 1-10,2019), not only do they aid in providing the desired electrical properties of the tissue, but they also help better understand the propagation of RF and microwave signals under different excitations and operating conditions.

articleTitle: Quantum Statistical Aspects of Emission and Absorption in Remote Sensing and Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Remote sensing and imaging of a scene through a channel that radiates, absorbs and scatters EM waves is best modelled using radiative transfer theory. In most studies on imaging, channel radiation and scattering is done in an ad hoc manner by incoherently adding the contributions in the overall channel model. We found that this approach can lead to substantial errors in several situations. To address this issue, we have developed a unified model for the channel transfer function. This properly takes into account multiple interactions between radiation and scattering. The channel is inhomogeneous with spatially varying temperature and density. It is well known that emission and absorptions lines strongly depend on temperature and pressure distributions. Thus, the statistics of emission and absorption coefficients are determined by the statistical distribution of channel temperature and density. Therefore, the signal intensity in the channel is governed by the radiative transfer equation (RTE) where the emission and absorption coefficients are their statistical average values. Moreover, the average emission coefficients are also spatially varying quantities albeit on a large scale. Hence, any correction to RTE must involve variance of emissivities. Spectral properties of common atmospheric gas species such as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{N}_{2}, \mathrm{O}_{2}, \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$</tex> and CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> at ambient ground temperature and pressure are readily available in the literature. Our interest is in investigating the emissivities of these and a few other species at nonstandard temperatures and pressures.

articleTitle: Speedy Assessment of Meteorological Equivalence for RF Propagation
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Mesoscale numerical weather predictions (NWP) are increasingly applied to radio-frequency (RF) propagation forecasts. Quantitative RF-skill metrics are not yet being tracked by operational forecast systems; however, the community generally agrees that modeling and computational improvements between ~2010 and 2020 resulted in semi-quantitative capabilities by the early 2020's. This trend is expected to continue as computational power grows and RF-significant upgrades are made to NWP model physics (e.g. finding and fixing dry-bias sources in boundary layer schemes).

articleTitle: Nearfield to Farfield Methods for Drone Beam Mapping
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Extracting cosmological 21 cm emission from the radio foregrounds which dominate requires precision calibration, including sub-percent measurements of the complex instrument beam. 21 cm cosmology experiments are typically driven to be compact transit interferometers with poor point-source sensitivity, and have found it difficult to constrain the beam shape to this precision with sky data alone. A technique that has been developed and demonstrated by multiple groups to address this is to transmit a calibrated RF signal from a drone into the telescope to measure the beam pattern.

articleTitle: Pulsed Non-coherent QPSK Low Probability of Intercept Waveforms for Commercial Software-Defined Radios
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Software-defined radios (SDRs) provide a quick way to modify a device's communication frequency, modulation, and functionality. This flexibility makes them a preferred choice for transceivers that require fast modification. This paper employs the SDR platform to create low-probability detection (LPD) links and build a clandestine network for operation in strong interference environments. Specifically, we develop a network with no common timing source between the transmitter and receiver. Previous research (D. R. Taylor, J. Walker, and B. Strunz, “Direct Sequence Spread Spectrum Experiments using GNU Radio Companion SDR,” in 2021 15th International Conference on Advanced Technologies, Systems and Services in Telecommunications, TELSIKS 2021 - Proceedings. Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers Inc., 2021, pp. 41–44) implemented LPD, non-coherent networks through SDRs, using only binary phase-shift keying (BPSK) and continuous streaming. This limits the amount of data sent, and even more importantly, the constant streaming makes the link easier to detect.

articleTitle: Transmission Through a Perforated Thick Metallic Screen
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The study of transmission through a perforated thick metallic screen has attracted the attention of numerous researchers. In broad terms, when the dimensions of the apertures or slots are significantly smaller than the wavelength in free space, transmission typically arises either through the resonance of the fundamental mode (known as Fabry-Perot resonance) or via high-order modes within the slot itself (referred to as Fano resonance). These structures are categorized as metasurfaces, which offer promising applications, including filters, absorbers, beam steering devices, sensors, and many more. Their compact size, lightweight nature, and capacity to conform to diverse surface shapes bestow metasurfaces with distinct advantages over alternative techniques employed for similar purposes.

articleTitle: Signal Classification for Spectrum Sharing with Machine Learning Using a Low-Cost SDR
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In the dynamic and ever-growing landscape of wireless networks, the intelligent detection and classification of signals are crucial for efficient spectrum sharing. A system that shares spectrum with signal knowledge can effectively allocate spectrum for various purposes such as dynamic channel access, computation, and interference mitigation. This study showcases the effectiveness and potential of machine learning algorithms in software defined radio (SDR) based spectrum sharing and classification, specifically focusing on LTE, WLAN, and 5G-new radio (NR) signals.

articleTitle: Generation of Super Low Frequency Signals at the HAARP Facility for Long Range Propagation
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Super low frequency electromagnetic radiation, or SLF, is defined as a frequency range of 30–300 Hz with wavelengths of 10,000-1,000 kilometers, respectively. SLF electromagnetic signals can be guided by the Earth-ionosphere waveguide and propagate over large distances. Since the waves are guided by the lower ionosphere, their propagation characteristics can serve as a diagnostic of the ionosphere's D region. The challenge of employing such waves in a controlled experiment comes down to the signal generation. To radiate such waves with a conventional antenna would require hardware that is many kilometers in length and impractical to build. To get around this limitation, the HAARP facility (High-frequency Active Auroral Research Program) located in Gakona Alaska, can be used to modulate natural overhead currents, known as the electrojet (quasi-DC electric current which flows in the D and E region of the Earth's ionosphere), which causes the upper atmosphere to act as a large antenna anywhere from 30–50 km in length. The HF antenna array at HAARP can produce SLF waves by modulating a high frequency beam at SLF.

articleTitle: Lower-Hybrid Waves and Nonlinear Whistler Wave Generation in Solar Flares*
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: In solar flares, simultaneous acceleration of both electrons and ions is observed despite the large mass difference between these species. In a flaring loop, ion velocity distributions can be formed with a ring-like structure either through shock formation, or via loss cone depletion [1]. These distributions are unstable to Lower-hybrid (LH) waves [2]. LH waves can simultaneously accelerate perpendicular-propagating ions and parallel-propagating electrons [1] because on LH timescales the ions are unmagnetized and the electrons are magnetized allowing for simultaneous resonance. However, these early studies did not look into the production of whistler waves in the presence of LH wave turbulence. As we show in this presentation, whistler waves are almost inevitable in the excitation of LH waves in low beta turbulent plasmas [3]. The generation mechanism of whistler waves in the solar wind (SW) is also an active area of research. The Parker Solar Probe (PSP) mission has enabled measurements of the SW at distances very close to the Sun. For example, [4] has confirm the excitation of whistler waves in the quiet SW at ~ 36 solar radii. And more recently, [5] shows the existence of broadband LH turbulence in the near solar wind (0.074 AU). However, the mechanisms of excitation of these waves are still debated and the causal linkage between LH waves and whistlers in the solar wind has not been studied. Here, we present results of 2-dimensional (2D) PIC simulations of nonlinear whistler wave generation by LH turbulence scattering by plasma particles. This nonlinear mechanism is sometimes known as either: induced scattering or nonlinear Landau damping. In our study, we generate the LH waves through an energetic ion ring velocity distribution, as in a solar flare, and study the impact of nonlinear scattering on the evolution of the instability. We show that the instability is saturated by the scattering of LH to whistler (W) waves. We present detailed analysis for the evolution of the LH and W waves. We also study the electron and ion velocity distribution functions (VDFs) and show their evolution in time. The simulation data analysis shows agreement with the whistlers being generated by the nonlinear induced scattering mechanism. Specifically, we identify the quasimodes (which are low frequency density perturbations driven by the ponderomotive force due to the beating of LH and W waves) and the individual constituent waves involved in the nonlinear induced scattering. <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">*</sup>This work was supported by the NRL Base Program.

articleTitle: Spectral Optical Theorem and Radiative Transport Equation in Random Media with Large Scale Fluctuations
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The optical theorem is a general law in scattering theory that relates the total scattering cross section of a scatterer to the imaginary part of its forward scattering amplitude. It turns out that this law is so fundamental that it extrapolates and permeates across several disciplines and physical processes with far-reaching implications. In the case of multiple scattering in random media the optical theorem relates the mass operator to the intensity operator. Note that the mass operator governs the mean Green's function while the intensity operator governs the coherence function in the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE). Tatarskii was among the first to derive the multiple scattering optical theorem for random media. We notice that the optical theorem that he used in applications is in the spatial domain. This is the version widely used in the literature.

articleTitle: Ionospheric Amplification of Whistler Mode Waves for Reduction of Radiation Belt Particle Populations
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Dedicated firing of rocket engines on satellites over ground VLF transmitters can be use to remove energetic electrons from radiation belts in the magnetosphere. This Rocket Exhaust Driven Amplification was demonstrated using a Cygnus burn over the Navy NML transmitter in North Dakota.

articleTitle: Design, Fabrication, and Experimental Characterization of an Ultra-Wideband, Electronically-Reconfigurable Transmitarray Element with High Peak and Average Power Handling Capability
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: High-power phased arrays have been widely used in radar, communications, and electronic warfare applications. Modern military applications such as electronic warfare and high-power radar systems often need high-power-capable phased arrays that can work over very wide bandwidths. Thus, the development of ultra-wide band, electronically reconfigurable phased arrays capable of handling a wide spectrum of high-power microwave sources is important. While many conventional phased array designs provide broad bandwidth or high radiation power levels, it is challenging to achieve both traits simultaneously. Active phased arrays can be very wideband but offer limited power handling capability (typically a few watts per element). Their nonlinear amplifiers can introduce significant RF distortion as the radiated power level increases and are subject to breakdown or thermal failure at elevated power levels. For this reason, most high-power phased arrays are passive phased arrays. All-metal passive phased arrays are especially high-power compatible, but they tend to suffer from narrow bandwidths of typically less than 20%-30%. In addition, their all-metal waveguide-based structures usually require relatively large profiles. For a full 2D array, the low-packing-density and large unit cell spacing causes grating lobe problems for such designs. The large size and weight of these all-metal-based phased arrays will limit their applications to large-size platforms.

articleTitle: Attenuation Of The Average Norton Surface Wave Propagating Along A Gently Undulating Surface
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Norton Surface Wave is an electromagnetic field that propagates along an unbounded, flat surface with a free space wavenumber but decaying in amplitude in a complicated manner. A worthwhile and concise review of the behavior of this field over a flat and a spherical surface is given in R. E. Collin's book Antennas and Radiowave Propagation. Because of the distances over which the Norton Surface Wave can propagate, it is very important to low frequency uses such as AM Broadcast. Unfortunately, the surface between the transmitter and receiver may be very gently undulating or nonplanar and this raises the question as to the integrity of the surface wave. That is, is the received field still obeying the predictions of Norton's analysis? One way to study this question is to record the received field in amplitude and phase at a fixed distance, with some small movement of the receiver to ensure that the phase is stable and then repeat this process at a different separation distance. The point of this measurement is to see if the measurements agree with Norton's theory. This has been done in the past, perhaps not as suggested here, and the results are not always in agreement with the predictions. That is, the measurements do not always result in a field amplitude that decays as 1/d<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> as predicted by Norton with proper accounting for the variation of the surface field with distance. The purpose of this paper is to show that if the wave traveling along the gently undulating surface does not radiate and is averaged, it is possible to introduce an additional exponential attenuation of the field strength as a function of distance This result is a consequence of the variation of the phase of the surface field along the surface-based path resulting from the surface undulations. The analysis is nearly exact with only one approximation involving the statistics of the process. It is important to realize this result is due to the phase of the field varying in a random fashion due to the along-path undulations but this manifest itself in a distance dependent attenuation of the propagating field. This result is for the average field, including phase, and is therefore seldom the case with many Norton surface wave applications. Finally, a discussion of how one might measure this effect is presented and discussed especially over terrain geometry as this is not a trivial consideration.

articleTitle: pycalc11: A Python Interface to the CALC VLBI Delay Model
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Accurate and precise delay models are essential to performing VLBI, especially in geodetic and astrometric applications. The CALC11 program has been a standard delay model in the VLBI world since the 1970s, aiming to provide geometric delays that are correct to picosecond precision. The difxcalc11 program provides an interface to CALC11 designed to work with the DiFX correlator, and updated the delay model to include new IERS parameters. Here, we present pycalc11, a Pythonic interface to the CALC11 program, derived from the difxcalc11 code base. In addition to providing a simpler interface that uses well-maintained astropy utilities, pycalc11provides users with direct access to underlying functions, and can lead to much more rapid development. We demonstrate pycalc11's consistency with difxcalc11 and with basic geometric delay calculations.

articleTitle: Facilitating Spectrum Sharing Between Passive and Active Users at a Prototype National Radio Dynamic Zone (NRDZ)
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A team comprising the University of Colorado, Boulder (CUB), the Hat Creek Radio Observatory (HCRO) and UC Berkeley (UCB) is presently engaged in National Science Foundation (NSF) funded research and development of various tools to facilitate co-existence of active and passive users of the electromagnetic spectrum, within a prototype National Radio Dynamic Zone (NRDZ) - centred around the Allen Telescope Array (ATA) at HCRO.

articleTitle: Space Weather Modeling at the University of Colorado Deep Learning Laboratory
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)

articleTitle: ngVLA Antenna Prototype Electronics and Radiometric Testing
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The MSIP (Mid-Scale Innovation Program) antenna is designed to prototype and test an 18m off-axis Gregorian telescope proposed for the ngVLA (next generation Very Large Array). The German company mtex is designing, fabricating and assembling this antenna at the ALMA (Atacama Large Millimeter Array) test site at the VLA (Very Large Array) in the Plains of San Agustin in New Mexico, US. The new antenna will be assembled and tested on the existing concrete pad and the site is being prepared with the appropriate infrastructure upgrades. The primary goal of this project is to document and test the antenna itself to determine if all ngVLA requirements and specifications have been met.

articleTitle: Active Low-Noise Matching with Subharmonic Parametric Amplifier
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: This paper presents a circuit simulation and numerical investigation of a circuit featuring a nonlinear inductor designed to induce subharmonic resonances. By incorporating the hysteresis effect of the nonlinear inductor, we successfully introduce and analyze this phenomenon within the circuit. The designed circuit is intended for use in the matching network of an electronically small antenna with the goal of improving antenna's noise performance through the implementation of the subharmonic parametric amplifier.

articleTitle: Near-Field MIMO RIS Channel Capacity
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The rapid evolution of wireless communication systems has ushered in an era of unprecedented connectivity and data transmission capabilities. Among the key technologies driving these advancements are Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) systems and Reflecting Intelligent Surfaces (RIS). On the one hand, MIMO harnesses the power of multiple antennas at both transmitter and receiver ends to exploit spatial diversity and multiplexing gains, enhancing data rates and signal reliability. On the other hand, RIS promise to enable precise manipulation of electromagnetic waves through intelligent reflecting elements. In this work we evaluate the Shannon point-to-point capacity of MIMO RIS systems, when all terminals have multiple antennas and have no limitation on the type of processing performed; in addition, our model includes near-field propagation effects.

articleTitle: RFI Considerations for the DSA-2000
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The DSA-2000 is a large astronomical survey in-terferometer currently being designed, and will be composed of 2,000 antennas spanning 700 - 2,000 MHz. The frequency coverage of the instrument makes it particularly vulnerable to Radio Frequency Interference as it overlaps with a high occupancy region of the spectrum. This paper describes the strategies employed to mitigate the effect of interference and ensure the scientific relevance of the telescope.

articleTitle: Investigating High-Gain in Gallium Nitride Photoconductive Switches
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Advances in the growth processes of wide bandgap (WBG) materials have allowed their emergence as a viable candidate for high-power switching. The photoconductive semiconductor switch (PCSS), has shown potential using gallium arsenide (GaAs), though power and lifetime limitations leave more to be desired. Using semi-insulated, doped gallium nitride (GaN) wafers, lateral geometries of PCSS have been produced and evaluated for operation under near IR laser incidence. At fields below 30 kV/cm, the lateral switch operates in the linear regime, (each absorbed photon produces one electron-hole pair), and photocurrent fitting the laser envelope is observed. Above this threshold, the switches demonstrate circuit-limited persistent conductivity (PC) or non-linear switching, where absorbed photons initiate what is presumed to be an avalanche process. The following document presents the results of the latest experiments made at the UNM to demonstrate high-gain mode operation in GaN-based PCSS.

articleTitle: Preliminary Findings of Stimulated Brillouin Scattering with Satellite Transmission

abstract: This paper describes an experiment to search for the missing piece of Stimulated Brillouin Scattering from the High Frequency Active Aurora Research Program (HAARP) experiment. articleTitle: mm-Wave UWB Tightly Coupled Dipole Array Realized Using a Hybrid PCB - 3D Printing Fabrication Approach
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The key challenge that hinders the realization of mmWave scanning apertures is associated with the fabrication, assembly, and measurement processes. Specifically, there are minimum fabricable feature size constraints for 3D structures. While planar monolithic arrays have been reported, their bandwidth is mainly limited by the height of the array. With this in mind, in this paper, we present a single 2–50 GHz array based on the concept of the tightly coupled dipole arrays (TCDAs). The presented mmWave TCDA uses capacitive overlaps to cancel the ground plane inductance and extend the bandwidth. The array operates across the 5G/6G allocated bands as well as the sub-6 GHz bands that offer lower propagation losses. The paper proposes to overcome the limitations of the PCB fabrication process by using a new hybrid assembly approach, that combines PCB fabrication with 3D printing. Notably, the novel approach follows a two-step process where the dipoles and the overlaps are printed on low-loss substrates with striplines. Then, the antenna boards are assembled vertically using a 3D printed board. The proposed fabrication method is compatible with commercially available 3D printing technology, leading to a simple and low-cost solution. Additionally, a compact double-Y balun is employed to achieve extremely low-cross polarization levels. Indeed, full-wave simulations reveal a continuous operation from 2–50 GHz with VSWR<3 and cross polarization isolation> 40 dB. Concurrently, the array has a very-low profile, where the dipole to ground plane distance is only 1/16 of the wavelength at the lowest frequency of operation. Finally, a prototype is fabricated and measured for operation at the frequencies of 2–40 GHz to validate the proposed fabrication approach.

articleTitle: Ionospheric Gradients Assessment for GBAS operations in Low-latitude Regions
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: The Global Positioning System (GPS) has an increasing role in air traffic control systems. However, the ionosphere may produce severe effects on the propagation of GPS signals. Consequently, the ionospheric effects cause positioning error that degrades the accuracy, performance and availability to support the phases of approach, landing, departure and surface operations of the aircraft, particularly in the equatorial and low-latitude regions. Different techniques and auxiliary systems have been developed to meet the safety requirements of aviation. For example, Ground Based Augmentation Systems (GBAS) provide higher accuracy for differential corrections. Differential corrections allow an aircraft approaching an airport to correct satellite navigation signals, removing spatially correlated errors. In addition, integrity parameters allow the aircraft system to calculate the limits of residual position errors and ensure safe operation.

articleTitle: Statistics of Electromagnetic Fields Excited in a Finite Length Cylindrical Cavity Under Longitudinal Aperture Position Uncertainties
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: A statistical description of the electromagnetic fields excited in a finite-length cylindrical cavity by plane wave incidence on a thin longitudinal aperture is provided for a stochastically described aperture location. A semi-analytical approach is used to represent cavity electric fields as a function of the longitudinal location of the aperture. This representation is then used to characterize the probability density function of the fields inside the cavity as a function of the probability density function (PDF) of the aperture position. Other field moments (e.g. mean, standard deviation, extreme values, etc.) can then be determined from the corresponding PDF. Results from the analytical approach are shown and validated through comparisons with Monte Carlo simulations.

articleTitle: Utilizing Distributed Circuit Topology Techniques to Achieve Reduced Maximum Branch Currents for High Power Impedance Matching RF Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: As the spectrum is becoming increasingly congested and contested due to spectrum reallocations for fifth-generation (5G) wireless communications, radar systems will need to be spectrum-agile while maintaining optimal performance over a wide range of frequencies to avoid incoming interferers. Radars changing operating frequency or array scan angle must maintain desirable detection range after reconfiguration. However, the optimal impedance match between the power amplifier (PA) and antenna changes as changes in frequency and antenna array scan angle occur, leading to a reduction in output power. A reconfigurable narrowband impedance tuner can provide an optimal match to maximize radar output power while system changes occur to avoid interference. Reconfigurable impedance tuners, however, must be capable of handling the high transmit power levels of typical radars, since the impedance tuner is placed directly after the PA in the transmit chain, and must possess minimal loss. With these two design requirements, many techniques have been researched to maximize power handling and minimize loss while possessing realtime switching speeds. However, efforts to realize an impedance tuner design with realtime switching speeds, low loss, and high-power handling have been limited. Previous work has demonstrated the main tradeoff between loss, power handling, and Smith Chart coverage (J. Roessler et al., “A Plasma-Switch Impedance Tuner With Microsecond Reconfiguration,” IEEE Transactions on Microwave Theory and Techniques, Vol. 71, No.1, January 2023, pp. 296–308). The constraints the tradeoff imposes can be reduced by optimizing the RF topology of an impedance tuner design.

articleTitle: Towards Enhanced Bandwidth in TWTs: An Exploration of Helix Structure Optimization
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Helix-based traveling wave tubes (TWT) is a microwave amplifier. TWTs have been widely used in various applications, such as wireless communication, plasma diagnostics, imaging, and healthcare, due to their high power, high efficiency, good linearity, and wide frequency ranges[1]. This work focuses on optimizing the helix slow wave structure of the TWT to get better bandwidth since it's cumbersome to operate TWT in high-power microwave frequency regimes.

articleTitle: Calculating Multi-Qubit Exchange Coupling Rates for Transmon Qubits Using a Field-Based Formalism
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Superconducting qubits are one of the most mature approaches to realize quantum computers. However, to meet the stringent performance requirements, these systems are becoming increasingly complex. To help solve this engineering problem, high-fidelity numerical methods are becoming a key resource. Unfortunately, existing approaches use full-wave computational electromagnetics (CEM) methods in inefficient ways that become impractical if even a few qubits are considered. Here, we derive a simple formula that can be efficiently evaluated using typical full-wave CEM tools to numerically calculate the exchange coupling rate between multiple transmons; which is a key system parameter involved in the design of multi-qubit entangling gates in modern quantum processors. Our approach is applicable to the common case of transmons operating in the dispersive regime where the operating frequency of the electromagnetic (EM) resonator is far detuned from the transition frequencies of the qubits coupled to it. We start from our field-theory description of these systems (T. E. Roth and W. C. Chew, “Macroscopic circuit quantum electrodynamics: A new look toward developing full-wave numerical models,” IEEE Journal on Multiscale and Multiphysics Computational Techniques, Vol. 6, 109-124,2021) with multiple qubits and perform a Schrieffer-Wolf transform to rewrite the system Hamiltonian into the dispersive regime. This re-expresses the indirect qubit-field coupling of the original Hamiltonian as direct qubit-qubit interactions with an exchange coupling rate that depends on properties of the EM system the qubits are embedded in. From here, typical field-theory techniques can be used to relate this exchange coupling rate to the EM Green's function, which can further be related to the impedance matrix between the qubits. This quantity can be efficiently computed with standard full-wave CEM tools, which is in contrast to prevailing approaches that rely on performing EM eigenmode decompositions. We qualitatively verified our formula using a geometry (Fig. 1, left) based on (Filipp, Stefan, et al. “Multimode mediated qubit-qubit coupling and dark-state symmetries in circuit quantum electrodynamics.” Physical Review A 83.6 (2011): 063827), and have also quantitatively tested it against other calculation methodologies (Fig. 2, right) (Solgun, Firat, David P. DiVincenzo, and Jay M. Gambetta. “Simple impedance response formulas for the dispersive interaction rates in the effective Hamiltonians of low anharmonicity superconducting qubits.” IEEE Transactions on Microwave Theory and Techniques 67.3 (2019): 928–948).

articleTitle: Recent Observations with the Mapper of the IGM Spin Temperature
publicationTitle: 2024 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM)
abstract: Measurements of redshifted 21-cm emission of neutral hydrogen have the potential to probe a wide range of epochs in the universe's history. At frequencies below ~150 MHz, redshifted 21-cm emission can open an observational window into cosmic dawn and the dark ages. The global 21-cm signal, averaged across the sky, captures the ignition and heating processes of the first stars and is expected to have a characteristic absorption feature around a red shift of 20. The first and only detection of the cosmic dawn absorption feature was reported by EDGES in 2018, and if confirmed to be true, represents our first point of entry into exploring this early epoch in our universe's history. However, the SARAS3 experiment recently reported a non-detection that is in tension with the EDGES result at roughly <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2\sigma$</tex>. Because global 21-cm observations require measurements of total power, experiments are limited by systematic uncertainties, rather than statistical noise. Independent measurement efforts are therefore crucial for further elucidating the cosmic dawn signal.
